manifest.author: LTM Cost IQ Methodology
manifest.questionDesign: Full 105-question CIO answer-experience redesign — CORE-01 to CORE-45 reviewed through v6.5; ADP-01 to ADP-20 reviewed in v6.6.
questionDesignPrinciples: CIO hypothesis is captured separately from engine findings and is not treated as evidence.
Initial assessment is hybrid: executive ranges/qualitative responses first; actuals and evidence are validated later.
Cost IQ and Value IQ are executive headline scores with confidence shown independently.
Economic opportunity and practical/actionable opportunity are distinct outputs.
Illustrative savings ranges require evidence validation before any savings commitment.
Stable IDs connect answer -> signal -> score -> finding -> opportunity -> recommendation -> LTM service.
Opportunity sizing distinguishes economic addressability from practical actionability using explicit feasibility constraints.
Trade-off, hypothesis, hotspot and context questions are used as signals and are not scored by option count or position.
Maturity scoring uses semantic option IDs rather than positional A/B/C mappings wherever a deterministic score is intended.

questions.prompt: Which areas of the technology estate account for a material share of technology cost today?
questions.intent: Establish the cost-relevant technology footprint so the assessment only activates diagnostics that are relevant to the enterprise.
questions.answerDesign: Select every area that materially contributes to technology cost. Do not select areas that are immaterial or purely incidental.
questions.evidenceImplication: Sets evidence scope

options.label: On-premises infrastructure and data centres
Private cloud / hosted private infrastructure
Public cloud services
VMware or other virtualization platforms
Colocation or third-party data-centre facilities
SaaS applications and subscriptions
Enterprise software and licensing
Network and connectivity
Data platforms, storage and analytics
Cybersecurity technology and security platforms
Internal technology workforce
External technology services / managed services
End-user computing and workplace technology
AI platforms, models and AI-enabled services
Other material technology spend

scoring.note: Scope trigger only; never score by number of areas selected. Feeds applicability routing (cloud findings only when PUBLIC_CLOUD or PRIVATE_CLOUD is selected; infrastructure questions ADP-09 to ADP-13 only when ON_PREM or PRIVATE_CLOUD) and the report scope statement. Keep required. When CORE-23 is merged into CORE-01 (BOUNDARY task 4) the merged question must keep the COLO, VMWARE and MANAGED options that CORE-23 has and CORE-01 lacks, or ADP-13 and ADP-09 lose their gating signal. Context facts never re-weight a score (GLOBAL-COVERAGE rule).
scoring.basis: Footprint question: which areas materially drive technology cost. It records a fact and routes applicability; scoring it would reward a longer or shorter list. Categories follow the TBM Taxonomy idea of IT towers (cost sources by technology area) but the option list itself is LTM heuristic; the TBM page summary does not list the towers (members-only), so alignment to named TBM towers is UNVERIFIED.

questions.answerGuidance: Think beyond the centrally managed IT estate where business-managed technology is material.

questions.prompt: Which industry most closely reflects the organization’s primary business model?
questions.intent: Select the industry context used to tailor later diagnostic questions and interpretation.
questions.answerDesign: Choose one primary industry; select the closest match where the organization spans multiple sectors.
questions.evidenceImplication: Determines relevant evidence areas

options.label: Banking / Financial Services
Insurance
Healthcare / Life Sciences
Manufacturing
Retail / Consumer
Energy / Utilities
Telecommunications
Technology
Travel / Transportation
Public Sector
Professional Services
Other

scoring.note: Sector records context and routes applicability and wording. It is never scored: ranking industries would be meaningless. Context facts never re-weight a score.
scoring.basis: LTM heuristic. A letter-keyed map that ranked the twelve industries from 100 to 20 never matched an option and scored nothing; it was removed (CQ3b).

questions.answerGuidance: Choose the industry that best describes the organization’s principal revenue-generating business.

questions.prompt: What is the organization’s approximate annual revenue?
questions.intent: Establish enterprise scale for interpreting technology economics and normalizing cost without requiring an exact financial figure.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the closest annual revenue band. Use the USD-equivalent band if the enterprise reports in another currency.
questions.evidenceImplication: Improves normalization

options.label: Below US$100M
US$500M–1B
US$1B–5B
US$5B–25B
Above US$25B
Not known / prefer not to disclose

questions.answerGuidance: A broad, recent estimate is sufficient; exact revenue is not required.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate annual technology spend currently in scope for this assessment?
questions.intent: Establish the financial baseline against which cost, value and opportunity signals will later be interpreted.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the closest spend band. Include material technology spend in scope even where it sits outside the central IT budget.
questions.evidenceImplication: Primary financial evidence input

options.label: Below US$5M
US$5M–25M
US$25M–50M
US$500M–1B
Above US$1B
Not known / prefer not to disclose

questions.answerGuidance: Use the figure leadership would consider the most representative current technology-spend baseline.

questions.prompt: Which categories are included in the technology-spend figure you just provided?
questions.intent: Test whether the financial baseline is complete enough to support credible cost and opportunity analysis.
questions.answerDesign: Select every category that is included in the reported spend figure. Use the reconciliation option when the boundary is unclear.
questions.evidenceImplication: Tests baseline completeness

options.label: Infrastructure and data centres
Public / private cloud
SaaS subscriptions
Software licences
Application development and support
Network and connectivity
Data platforms and analytics
Cybersecurity
Internal technology workforce
External services and systems integrators
Workplace / end-user computing
Other material technology spend
I cannot confidently reconcile what is included

scoring.note: Do not score by selection count. Feeds (a) the evidence-confidence flag on the spend baseline when UNKNOWN is selected, (b) a report line listing areas selected in CORE-01 but missing here (CORE-01 minus CORE-05, computed in the report layer, not in scoreQuestion), (c) F-001 evidence text only; no new trigger. Keep required. UNKNOWN must be exclusive of the other options (check the control). Context facts never re-weight a score (GLOBAL-COVERAGE rule).
scoring.basis: Records what the spend figure in CORE-04 includes. A count of categories cannot be scored (the question says not to, and a smaller estate legitimately includes fewer categories). The useful reading is a comparison: categories material in CORE-01 but not included here show a baseline that understates spend; UNKNOWN shows the baseline cannot be reconciled. LTM heuristic; no published benchmark.

questions.answerGuidance: Answer based on what is actually included in the number you gave in CORE-04, not what should ideally be included.

questions.prompt: How confident are you that the technology-spend baseline is complete enough to support executive decisions, including material business-led technology spend?
questions.intent: Separate confidence in the data baseline from the maturity of the cost-management process.
questions.answerDesign: Rate confidence, not performance. Five cumulative stars represent increasing confidence in completeness and reconciliation.
questions.evidenceImplication: Requests validation of excluded spend

labels: Significant gaps are likely
Several material gaps remain
Most major spend is visible, but gaps remain
Broadly complete, with limited gaps
Comprehensive and reconciled

questions.answerGuidance: Think about omissions, indirect spend, business-led technology and inconsistent cost ownership.

questions.prompt: Looking ahead 12–24 months, which three technology outcomes should receive the strongest protection when trade-offs are made?
questions.intent: Capture the CIO’s explicit investment priorities and the outcomes that should be protected when cost and value trade-offs are made.
questions.answerDesign: Select exactly three outcomes, then rank those three from highest to lowest priority.
questions.evidenceImplication: Links investment priorities to roadmap

options.label: Reduce recurring run cost while protecting service levels
Increase measurable business value from technology
Modernize aging platforms and infrastructure
Accelerate strategic and digital transformation
Increase resilience, continuity and recoverability
Strengthen cybersecurity and reduce technology risk
Scale AI / GenAI into priority business use cases
Reduce technology complexity and technical debt
Improve employee productivity through better technology
Increase the ability to redirect technology as priorities change

scoring.note: Feeds the report narrative and the ordering of recommendations (those serving a protected outcome are listed first). No score impact. Keep required. Context facts never re-weight a score (GLOBAL-COVERAGE rule).
scoring.basis: A ranking of three outcomes the CIO would protect. It records a priority, not a better-to-worse condition; ranking position cannot be a score. Consequence: VALUE-01 Business Alignment still has no scored question after this batch (it had none before), so a VALUE-01 score cannot be shown until a scored question is added (see ADP-33 and CORE-14/17 for candidates outside this batch). LTM heuristic.

questions.answerGuidance: Rank outcomes that should survive funding pressure—not activities that are simply important today.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the cost pressure leadership expects technology to manage over the next 12 months?
questions.intent: Distinguish routine efficiency expectations from a formal, urgent or investment-constraining cost mandate.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the single statement that best reflects the current executive mandate.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: High cost pressure activates cost-reduction deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Sets urgency

options.label: Cost is monitored, but there is no material executive pressure to reduce it.
Efficiency expectations are increasing and leaders want visible improvement.
Technology cost reduction is an explicit executive priority for the next 12 months.
Significant savings are expected within the next 12 months and difficult trade-offs are already underway.
Cost pressure is already constraining investment in strategic technology priorities.

scoring.note: The cost pressure leadership expects technology to absorb. An external condition, not a maturity of practice; it orders the recommendations and the report narrative. No score.
scoring.basis: LTM heuristic. A letter-keyed map never matched an option and scored nothing; it was removed (CQ3b).

questions.answerGuidance: Select the situation leadership is actually managing, rather than the level of cost pressure you think it should have.

questions.prompt: Before seeing any assessment findings, where would you expect the largest opportunities to improve technology value? Select up to five areas, then rank the three you would investigate first.
questions.intent: Capture the CIO’s starting hypothesis before the diagnostic engine presents its own findings, enabling useful comparison between perception and evidence.
questions.answerDesign: Select up to five areas that appear promising; rank the three you would investigate first.
questions.evidenceImplication: Creates hypothesis list

options.label: Retire or consolidate low-value, duplicate or overlapping technology
Improve cloud consumption, architecture and platform economics
Improve technology workforce productivity and capacity utilization
Improve supplier commercials, scope and sourcing economics
Improve economics and outcomes from data and AI investments
Reduce complexity, duplication and technical debt
Automate manual technology operations and service activities
Improve product engineering and delivery economics
Improve measurement and realization of technology benefits
Align technology spend more tightly to business priorities

scoring.note: Feeds a "your hypothesis versus the findings" panel in the executive report (build is a CQ5 item). No score impact. Keep required. Context facts never re-weight a score (GLOBAL-COVERAGE rule).
scoring.basis: The question already declares itself a CIO starting hypothesis with no score impact (hypothesisRole, hypothesisComparison). It is a selection of areas plus a ranking, so scoring would invent an order. The comparison with engine-identified opportunity areas is configured but not built in the report (VALIDATION section 6). LTM heuristic. Note CLOUD_PLATFORM_EFFICIENCY is kept as a hypothesis option; it routes to FinOps IQ and does not bring cloud practice depth back into Cost IQ.

questions.answerGuidance: This is your hypothesis—not the assessment conclusion. Choose areas where you would expect better value, lower waste or stronger outcomes.
questions.hypothesisComparison: Compare selected/ranked areas with engine-identified opportunity areas in executive report; no score impact.

questions.prompt: Which change in the way technology is funded would most improve the value you can get from the current budget?
questions.intent: Identify the structural funding change that would most improve transparency, outcome accountability, flexibility or portfolio discipline.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the one funding-model change that would have the greatest practical effect.
questions.evidenceImplication: May require governance evidence

options.label: Make spend, allocations and unit costs more transparent so leaders can challenge trade-offs.
Tie funding more directly to measurable business outcomes and benefits.
Make a larger share of funding easier to redirect as priorities change.
Move suitable funding from projects toward products / services with ongoing accountability.
Use enterprise portfolio governance to stop lower-value demand and reallocate funds.
Clarify which funding decisions belong with central IT, business or product teams.
The current funding model is broadly fit for purpose.

scoring.note: A preference for one funding-model change; an order of the options is not a maturity score.

questions.answerGuidance: Choose the change that would most improve decision quality or redirectability of existing spend.

questions.prompt: When business priorities change materially, which statement best describes how quickly you can redirect technology funding and capacity?
questions.intent: Assess strategic agility and identify structural commitments that make technology funding and capacity difficult to redirect.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement that best describes the normal operating reality—not an exceptional case.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Low agility activates funding deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Requires commitment/contract evidence

options.label: We can redirect discretionary funding and capacity within weeks.
We can redirect a meaningful portion within one quarter through normal governance.
Redirection requires significant reprioritization and usually spans multiple quarters.
Most funding or capacity is tied up in existing contracts, platforms or run commitments.
Redirecting funding or capacity is currently difficult and creates major disruption.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider funding commitments, contracts, platform run costs, delivery capacity and governance lead time.

questions.prompt: When you need to explain where technology money goes, how far can you take that analysis today?
questions.intent: Assess whether leaders can move from a total technology spend figure to a reliable view of categories, owners, services and business use.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement that best reflects the level of spend transparency available today.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate enterprise spend baseline, material business-led spend and reconciliation logic.

options.label: We can reconcile enterprise technology spend to major categories, owners, services/products and material business-led spend.
We have an enterprise view, but some material business-led, indirect or shared spend remains outside it.
We can see major spend categories, but allocation to services, products or business units is inconsistent.
We mainly see spend by vendors, towers, departments or projects and struggle to build an enterprise picture.
We do not have a reliable enterprise technology spend baseline.

scoring.note: Direct maturity signal for Spend Transparency.

questions.answerGuidance: Answer from what leaders can actually see and reconcile today — not what finance, IT or procurement intends to build.
questions.opportunityImplication: Strengthen the enterprise technology spend baseline before sizing optimization opportunities.
questions.confidenceImpact: Baseline completeness materially affects confidence in downstream opportunity sizing.

questions.prompt: At what level can technology cost be routinely understood and challenged today?
questions.intent: Assess whether cost is traceable to a useful management object rather than only accounting or procurement categories.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the description closest to how cost is managed in the majority of the estate.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate allocation rules, service catalog/unit-cost models, cost-centre mappings and material exceptions.

options.label: By service/product, with clear owners, consumers and major cost drivers or unit economics.
By business unit or business-facing product, with useful allocation but limited unit-cost detail.
By technology tower/platform, with limited allocation to consumers or services.
Primarily through vendors, contracts or procurement categories rather than the services they support.
Primarily through projects/programs, with weak visibility into ongoing service economics.
Primarily through general-ledger categories or cost centres.
Several models coexist, but practice varies materially across the estate.

scoring.note: Score reflects decision usefulness of cost attribution, not preference for a specific accounting model.

questions.answerGuidance: Focus on the level leaders can routinely use to understand cost drivers and make decisions.
questions.opportunityImplication: Identify cost pools where improved allocation would expose leakage or enable business/value trade-offs.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low allocation traceability reduces confidence in category-level opportunity sizing.

questions.prompt: Which material technology cost areas are hardest to attribute to a clear owner, service/product or cost driver?
questions.intent: Identify where allocation and ownership gaps are concentrated so later diagnostics can focus on material leakage rather than asking the same questions everywhere.
questions.answerDesign: Select all material problem areas. Select 'None material' only when allocation is broadly workable.
questions.evidenceImplication: Request category-specific allocation evidence only for selected areas.

options.label: Cloud consumption / shared cloud platforms
Shared infrastructure / data-centre platforms
SaaS subscriptions and shared licences
Enterprise software and licensing
Network and connectivity
Data platforms, storage and analytics
Cybersecurity and security platforms
Internal technology workforce
External services / systems integrators / managed services
Applications and product teams
Other material shared technology cost
None material — attribution is broadly workable

scoring.note: Do not score by number of selections. Use selected categories to activate evidence and leakage diagnostics.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about material spend that leaders cannot explain beyond a shared pool, vendor, tower or departmental budget.
questions.opportunityImplication: Use selected categories to target visibility and allocation leakage assessment.
questions.confidenceImpact: Selected gaps lower confidence for opportunity sizing in the affected cost pools.

questions.prompt: How quickly can executives obtain a consolidated technology cost view that is current enough to act on?
questions.intent: Assess whether cost intelligence arrives with a cadence and freshness that supports intervention rather than retrospective reporting.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the normal operating cadence and usability level.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate reporting cadence, data freshness, reconciliations and examples of decisions made from the cost view.

options.label: Self-service/current dashboards are available when leadership needs them, with sufficiently fresh data.
A monthly view is available and includes enough context to challenge major movements.
A quarterly view is available and is mainly used for management or budget reviews.
The consolidated view is mainly available twice a year or during planning cycles.
The view is primarily annual or part of the formal budget process.
A consolidated view is assembled mainly when a specific issue, renewal or escalation occurs.
There is no dependable consolidated executive technology cost view.

scoring.note: Cadence is one contributor to governance maturity; data quality still drives confidence separately.

questions.answerGuidance: Choose how the information actually works for leadership today, including whether it is current enough to challenge significant movements.
questions.opportunityImplication: Improve cost intelligence cadence where slow or ad hoc reporting delays intervention.
questions.confidenceImpact: Poor cadence can limit evidence timeliness even when a baseline exists.

questions.prompt: Is material technology spend initiated, owned or controlled outside the central technology organization?
questions.intent: Identify business-led or decentralized technology spend that may create visibility, duplication or governance gaps.
questions.answerDesign: Answer whether material spend exists outside central technology; use unsure where the boundary cannot be confidently established.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate decentralized procurement, finance records, SaaS inventories and business-owned technology.

options.label: Yes — material business-led or decentralized technology spend exists.
No — material technology spend is centrally governed or reconciled.
We cannot confidently determine the amount outside central technology.

scoring.note: This is a scope/governance trigger, not a direct maturity score.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider SaaS, data/AI, local applications, departmental platforms, engineering tools and externally procured technology that may not sit in the central IT budget.
questions.opportunityImplication: Assess shadow-tech duplication, commercial leakage and governance gaps where material spend sits outside central IT.
questions.confidenceImpact: Unknown decentralized spend materially reduces confidence in the enterprise baseline.

questions.prompt: Approximately what percentage of technology spend can be traced to a clear owner, service/product and primary cost driver?
questions.intent: Quantify attribution coverage directly without requiring an exact enterprise allocation calculation.
questions.answerDesign: Use a best defensible percentage estimate; exact precision is not required.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate allocation coverage for the largest spend pools and material exceptions.
questions.answerGuidance: Estimate the share of spend where leadership can identify who owns it, what service/product it supports and the main driver of cost. Use Unknown when a percentage would be misleading.
questions.opportunityImplication: Focus deeper diagnostic effort where spend remains unattributed or pooled.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low traceability lowers confidence in category-level economic conclusions.

questions.prompt: When technology spend no longer delivers the expected value, how strong are the decision rights to challenge, reduce or stop it?
questions.intent: Assess whether enterprise governance has practical authority to act on underperforming spend.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement closest to what can actually happen, not merely what policy allows.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate governance charter, decision rights, examples of challenged investments and stop/reduce decisions.

options.label: Cross-enterprise portfolio governance can challenge, reduce or stop spend across business and technology.
Technology leadership can challenge or stop discretionary technology spend within a defined mandate.
Finance/procurement can challenge defined categories, contracts or budgets, but not always the underlying demand.
Budget or service owners can challenge spend within their own area, with limited enterprise intervention.
There is no consistent decision right; exceptions, commitments or business dependencies usually prevail.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about whether leaders can challenge funding, reduce scope, stop renewals or redirect capacity when evidence shows value is weak.
questions.opportunityImplication: Establish a repeatable challenge mechanism for low-value or underperforming spend.
questions.confidenceImpact: Weak challenge evidence increases uncertainty around the practicality of identified rationalization opportunities.

questions.prompt: For a material technology investment, which evidence is routinely required before funding is approved?
questions.intent: Assess whether investment decisions are supported by sufficient economic, outcome, risk and operating evidence before money is committed.
questions.answerDesign: Select the evidence that is routinely required in the normal approval process. Do not select items required only for exceptional investments.
questions.evidenceImplication: Request a sample of recent investment approvals and compare stated requirements with actual evidence used.

options.label: Clear strategic/business rationale and expected contribution
Business case with alternatives and investment rationale
Total cost of ownership / lifecycle cost
Quantified expected benefits with accountable owners
Risk, security, resilience or regulatory impact
Architecture, dependency and technology impact
People, operating model and capacity impact
Commercial options, sourcing and contractual analysis
Defined outcome metrics, baseline and post-delivery measurement plan
No consistent evidence set is required across material investments

scoring.note: Do not score by simple option count; evaluate combinations and required evidence patterns in the deterministic engine.

questions.answerGuidance: Choose what approval bodies consistently see, not what a strong business case would ideally contain.
questions.opportunityImplication: Strengthen investment discipline where economic or benefit evidence is missing before funding.
questions.confidenceImpact: Weak pre-investment evidence reduces confidence in portfolio-level value conclusions.

questions.prompt: After a major technology investment goes live, what normally happens to the business outcomes that were expected?
questions.intent: Assess whether benefits are owned, measured and acted upon after implementation.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the operating reality for the majority of material investments.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate benefit registers, post-implementation reviews, KPI baselines/targets and examples of corrective action.

options.label: Benefits have accountable owners, baselines, targets, review dates and action when outcomes miss.
Benefits are tracked for the largest investments, but not consistently across the portfolio.
Benefits are estimated in the business case but are rarely revisited after delivery.
We mainly track delivery, adoption or usage metrics rather than business outcomes.
There is no systematic process for checking whether expected benefits were achieved.

questions.answerGuidance: Focus on what happens after delivery — including whether misses trigger corrective action, scope changes or future funding decisions.
questions.opportunityImplication: Improve benefits realization and use outcome evidence to redirect future technology investment.
questions.confidenceImpact: Weak benefit measurement reduces confidence in Value IQ and in opportunities framed as value realization.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches how most technology investment and run spend is funded today?
questions.intent: Understand the structural funding model and the constraints it creates for cost ownership, value management and redirection.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the dominant model; mixed models are acceptable where the estate genuinely operates differently by domain.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate budget structures, funding commitments, reallocation rules, run/change split and examples of in-year funding movement.

options.label: Funding is primarily tied to products/services and measurable business outcomes.
Funding is primarily tied to technology services and their consumption or service economics.
Funding is primarily organized around projects and programs, with limited ongoing product/service ownership.
Funding is primarily assigned to technology towers or platforms.
Most funding is locked into annual budgets with limited reallocation during the year.
Different funding models coexist and the enterprise has no clearly dominant model.

scoring.note: Model type is not judged in isolation; score should be reconciled with actual redirectability and governance evidence.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider how funding is actually committed and governed across run, change, products/services and major programs.
questions.opportunityImplication: Identify structural funding constraints that prevent investment redirection or continuation of low-value spend.
questions.confidenceImpact: Funding rigidity is a practical constraint that should moderate actionable opportunity, not erase economic opportunity.

questions.prompt: When a technology product, service or investment underperforms, what normally happens next?
questions.intent: Assess whether portfolio governance creates a repeatable intervention path before weak performance becomes entrenched spend.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern that best describes normal practice.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate portfolio review cadence, intervention thresholds and examples where funding/scope/ownership changed after performance review.

options.label: Performance/value thresholds trigger formal review and intervention, including reduce, redirect or stop decisions.
Formal portfolio reviews occur at least annually and can result in funding or scope changes.
Challenge mainly occurs during budget, planning or renewal cycles.
Intervention usually starts only after costs, delivery or business dissatisfaction become problematic.
Underperforming spend is rarely challenged or materially changed.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about the trigger for intervention and whether leaders can change funding, scope, ownership or continuation.
questions.opportunityImplication: Create portfolio challenge and stop/reduce mechanisms to prevent low-value spend from persisting.
questions.confidenceImpact: Weak intervention history lowers confidence that economically attractive rationalization is practically executable.

questions.prompt: How confidently can you match major SaaS subscriptions to active usage and business need before renewal?
questions.intent: Assess whether SaaS economics are driven by actual usage and business need rather than purchased seat counts alone.
questions.answerDesign: Rate the level of confidence leadership has in using usage and business-need evidence before major SaaS renewals.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Deepens SaaS economics diagnostic when SAAS is selected
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate major subscriptions using user counts, utilization telemetry, business-owner confirmation and renewal decisions.
questions.findingImplication: Low confidence may indicate unused or poorly aligned SaaS spend.

options.label: Usage is continuously measured and licences are adjusted as demand changes.
Utilization is reviewed before major renewals and meaningful reductions are made.
Some major products have utilization data, but coverage is inconsistent.
We mainly manage licence counts and contracts rather than actual usage.
Actual utilization is largely unknown.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider active users, feature utilization, business-owner validation, overlapping products and whether renewal quantities change based on evidence.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate SaaS licence right-sizing and renewal challenge analysis.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; test against usage and renewal evidence.

labels.1: Usage and business need are largely unknown
labels.2: We know basic seat counts, but usage evidence is limited
labels.3: Major products have useful usage data, but reviews are inconsistent
labels.4: Major renewals are usually challenged using usage and business-owner evidence
labels.5: Usage and business need routinely drive subscription quantities and renewal decisions

questions.prompt: When two SaaS products provide overlapping capability, what normally happens?
questions.intent: Assess whether overlapping SaaS capability is identified and converted into portfolio decisions.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern that best describes what happens when meaningful SaaS overlap is identified.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using application inventory, capability maps, contracts and consolidation decisions.
questions.findingImplication: Weak challenge of overlapping capability can indicate SaaS or portfolio leakage.

options.label: Enterprise portfolio governance actively consolidates overlapping products and tracks the value released.
Major overlaps are reviewed by the relevant business and technology owners and consolidation decisions are made when justified.
Overlap is documented, but decisions are inconsistent or depend on local owners.
Overlap is mainly challenged when a renewal or significant cost event is approaching.
There is no consistent process to identify and rationalize overlapping SaaS capability.
We do not have enough visibility to identify meaningful SaaS overlap reliably.

questions.answerGuidance: Focus on whether overlap leads to consolidation, ownership decisions and measurable value release—or simply gets documented.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate duplicate-SaaS consolidation opportunity sizing.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; validate material overlap and actual decisions.

questions.prompt: When cloud or SaaS demand changes, how much practical flexibility do you have to change major commercial commitments?
questions.intent: Separate commercial economics from practical feasibility by identifying contractual lock-in affecting optimization.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement that best reflects what the organization can realistically change—not what contracts theoretically permit.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Deepens commercial economics diagnostic when PUBLIC_CLOUD or SAAS is selected
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate major commitments using contracts, renewal calendars, commitment utilization and change/termination clauses.
questions.findingImplication: Material lock-in can create commercial leakage and constrain otherwise attractive optimization actions.

options.label: Commitments can be actively re-sized, reallocated or changed as demand changes, with limited commercial friction.
Most commitments are reviewed routinely and material changes can usually be negotiated or rebalanced.
Some commitments are flexible, but material changes often wait for defined commercial windows.
Major commitments materially limit near-term flexibility; renewal or contract events drive most change.
Contractual lock-in materially constrains optimization decisions and creates significant execution friction.
The organization does not have dependable visibility into the terms or flexibility of major commitments.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider committed spend, minimums, termination rights, renewal dates, price protections, portability and the ability to reduce or reallocate commitments without major disruption.
questions.opportunityImplication: Report economic opportunity separately from practical opportunity where contractual lock-in reduces near-term actionability.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium until major commitments and contract terms are evidenced.

questions.prompt: Which software and licensing areas warrant the strongest economic or compliance review?
questions.intent: Identify licensing domains most likely to contain cost, compliance or renewal exposure.
questions.answerDesign: Select areas where spend, usage uncertainty, contract exposure, audit risk or renewal activity makes deeper review worthwhile.
questions.evidenceImplication: Use entitlement records, deployment/usage evidence, contracts, audit history and renewal calendars.
questions.findingImplication: Selected categories become targeted licensing economics hotspots.

options.label: Database platforms and database licensing
Virtualization platforms, including VMware
ERP and other major enterprise applications
Operating systems and infrastructure software
Middleware, integration and data-platform licensing
Security and compliance software
Developer, engineering and specialist tools

More than 10 major overlapping platforms

The FinOps Licensing and SaaS capability states a review process for new SaaS requests so teams do not buy duplicates, and requires FinOps involvement when licences or SaaS are acquired outside cloud providers (Walk), but gives no percentage. The 30% F-017 trigger is an LTM heuristic and UNSOURCED: a widely quoted "shadow IT" share exists in analyst commentary but I could not verify a primary source with method and sample, so none is cited. The owner should treat 30 as adjustable. Slider has no option map; the engine path is normalize invert-0-100. The page cannot record "Unknown" on a slider (VALIDATION section 6), so an unanswered slider is simply unscored, never rated as good.

The prompt says "How confident are you" while the anchors describe practice; consider "How well is" (minor, owner optional). Needs applicability gating (ON_PREM).

2 — Capacity data exists, but major sizing decisions are still uncertain

4 — Capacity is routinely matched to forecast demand with limited excess
5 — Capacity is actively optimized against demand, resilience and forecast growth

findings.title: Technology workforce capacity may not align to demand

findings.title: Vendor economics may contain commercial leakage

findings.title: Complexity and technical debt are contributing to run cost

recommendations.title: Establish an Enterprise Technology Spend Baseline
recommendations.description: Create a reconciled view of technology spend across major categories, ownership and material business-led spend.

recommendations.title: Launch Cost & Value Governance
recommendations.description: Create repeatable decision rights and challenge mechanisms linking technology spend to value, risk and strategic priorities.

recommendations.title: Run a Cloud Economics Diagnostic
recommendations.description: Validate demand alignment, rightsizing, commitment strategy, tagging and consumption governance before sizing any savings opportunity.

recommendations.title: Run SaaS & Licensing Rationalization
recommendations.description: Validate utilization, entitlements, overlap, contract terms and renewal timing across SaaS and major software vendors.

recommendations.title: Optimize Infrastructure Footprint
recommendations.description: Validate capacity, utilization, lifecycle and facility/network economics to identify optimization and avoidance opportunities.

recommendations.title: Optimize Workforce & Operations
recommendations.description: Align demand, skills, sourcing and automation to improve productivity and reduce avoidable run effort.

recommendations.title: Reset Vendor Strategy
recommendations.description: Review strategic vendors, commercial structures, sourcing mix and performance governance to improve leverage and outcomes.

recommendations.title: Rationalize Application & Technology Portfolio
recommendations.description: Prioritize applications and platforms using cost, business value, risk and complexity to simplify the estate.

recommendations.title: Institutionalize Benefits Realization
recommendations.description: Set measurable benefit baselines, targets and post-implementation reviews for major technology investments.

recommendations.title: Build a 12–24 Month Investment Roadmap
recommendations.description: Sequence cost, productivity and reinvestment actions around business priorities, dependencies and organizational realities.
